gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the two picks' cycle ratings share the same 80% end-of-life basis (Pecron E1000LFP 3,500+ cycles, BLUETTI Elite 100 mini 6,000+ cycles), which gives the $379 BLUETTI about 1.7x the Pecron's rated lifetime energy, or that the "1,400W" on the BLUETTI's listing is a resistive-only Power Lifting figure and not continuous output.
standout_why: Compared against PopSci's Black Friday deals page (the cited one), OutletPicks' 1,000–1,299Wh page and Backup Power Hub's Black Friday tracker, all opened 2026-11-27. PopSci gives the Elite 100 mini's "more than 6,000 charge cycles" with no end-of-life percentage and does not list the Pecron E1000LFP at all. OutletPicks prints "Power Lifting 1400W" beside 700W with no explanation and gives no cycle figure for any unit. Backup Power Hub gives one output figure per model, no surge/continuous split and no cycle basis. ChatGPT's own answer already states 1,800W vs 700W continuous, so the output split is not new; the same-basis cycle comparison and the lifting footnote are.
decides: It confirms the split rather than overturning it. The Pecron E1000LFP ($399) is still the only one of ChatGPT's two picks that clears the 1,500W kettle/heater line on continuous watts. But both ratings are to 80%, so for a shopper who cycles daily on loads under 700W the Elite 100 mini's 6,000+ against 3,500+ is a like-for-like 1.7x life advantage for $20 less. The 1,400W Power Lifting figure does not move the Elite 100 mini across the 1,500W line: it applies to resistive appliances only and is still under 1,500W. The DJI Power 1000 V2 (Amazon $379.99) could not be normalised because DJI's spec pages would not open, so the desk's DJI #1 placement is neither confirmed nor contradicted on this angle.
